fetched_contents.text: Effects of freeze–thaw cycles on the deformation and microstructure of silt Introduction With the construction of highways and railways in seasonally frozen regions, the issue of damage to engineering structures caused by freeze–thaw cycles has attracted widespread attention worldwide (Jin et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2019; Wang and Chen, 2024). Under the influence of external climate conditions, subgrade soil within the range of the freezing layer in seasonally frozen regions undergoes periodic frost heave and thaw settlement-induced compressive deformation, leading to subgrade diseases (Cui et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024). Under the action of freeze–thaw cycles, the internal physical structure and mechanical properties of the soil vary continuously (Zhou et al., 2020), leading to the evolution and development of macroscopic deformation. To study the intrinsic evolution mechanism, it is necessary to clarify the transport of water and heat within the soil (Hao et al., 2023; Niu et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2021; Xia et al., 2023) and gain a comprehensive understanding of the deformation development during this process. Previous studies have primarily conducted laboratory tests on soil columns subjected to freeze–thaw cycles to investigate the coupled water–heat transfer and deformation behavior of soils (Wei et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Conventional freeze–thaw tests commonly employ displacement sensors or linear variable differential transformers installed on the surface of soil columns to monitor deformation. While being effective at capturing overall deformation trends, these methods lack spatial resolution and cannot resolve internal strain heterogeneity (Wang and Chen, 2024; Zhai et al., 2023). Therefore, a method that can provide localized deformation measurements throughout the entire soil column during freezing and thawing remains a critical research need. The particle image velocimetry (PIV) technique, a noncontact optical measurement method, enables high-resolution tracking of internal displacement and has been increasingly used in frost heave studies (White et al., 2003; Hao et al., 2023). PIV allows for the visualization of localized deformation zones and provides insights into how temperature, water content, and ice formation affect strain localization. Although PIV is now being applied to frozen soil mechanics (Li et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2020a; Zhang et al., 2023a; Zhang et al., 2023b), its application in freeze–thaw cycle testing remains limited. In parallel, microstructural studies using SEM or MIP have been widely employed to investigate pore-scale changes in frozen soils (Sun et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2022). However, these techniques are typically conducted post hoc and are not representative of real-time deformation processes, limiting their ability to capture the dynamic interaction between structural evolution and mechanical response. To our knowledge, this study is among the first to integrate PIV with SEM and MIP techniques in a unified experimental framework for freeze–thaw cycle testing. By coupling in situ strain field measurement with pore structure evolution tracking, this research bridges the existing gap in our understanding of the link between microstructural evolution and macroscopic deformation mechanisms in silty soil. The freeze–thaw process leads to a rearrangement of the soil particle structure, which macroscopically manifests as increased heterogeneity and anisotropy, resulting in a soil structure that is either loose or dense. The microscopic manifestations include broken particle connections and significant changes in the porosity (Li et al., 2024b; Kühn et al., 2021). Therefore, the changes in the macroscopic structure of the soil are closely linked to changes in its microstructure, which can be used to explain its macroscopic properties. Currently, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP) are commonly used to analyze the microstructure of frozen soil (Sun et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2019; Schlüter et al., 2022; Fan et al., 2022). Previous studies have predominantly explored the effects of freeze–thaw cycles on soil properties from either the perspective of macroscopic deformation or microstructural evolution, often in isolation. However, comprehensive research integrating quantitative full-field to local cross-scale deformation measurement techniques with microstructural analysis methods—such as SEM and MIP—remains limited. This paper proposes an innovative research approach that employs PIV to accurately capture deformation field variations in silty soil during freeze–thaw cycles. By coupling this with microstructural evolution analysis, the study establishes a direct link between macroscopic deformation characteristics and underlying micro-mechanisms, thus providing new theoretical support for elucidating the fundamental mechanical behavior of silty soil under freeze–thaw conditions. In summary, conventional experimental studies on the freeze–thaw cycles of soil columns have typically focused on the macroscopic deformation of the soil; a comprehensive study of the local deformation and microstructure is lacking. This study aimed to systematically reveal the relationship between local deformation and microstructural changes in soil under freeze–thaw cycles by combining the PIV technique and the microstructural analysis. First, the PIV technique was utilized to accurately measure the local deformation. Subsequently, the SEM and MIP techniques were combined for an in-depth study of the microstructural evolution under freeze–thaw cycles and its influence on macroscopic deformation. fetched_contents.text: Experimental and analytical investigation on frost heave characteristics of an unsaturated moderately expansive clay Highlights * • Frost heave tests of unsaturated moderately expansive clay in open system was carried out. * • The SCS stage occurs in expansive clay with a decrease of frost depth lagging behind. * • Dramatic vertical displacement of unfrozen zone due to freezing-induced water flux is observed. * • A physico-empirical approach is proposed to predict the freezing point depression. Abstract Expansive clay, a kind of clayey soil, is widely distributed in seasonally frozen regions. Numerous studies have attempted to explain the frost heave characteristics of clayey soils, but few of them have paid attention to the frost heave characteristics of unsaturated expansive clay, especially considering the influence of swelling properties. In this study, a series of freezing temperature tests and step-freezing tests on an unsaturated moderately expansive clay and a silty clay were conducted. The silty clay was taken as a reference. The testing program, experimental results are presented and discussed, especially to the freezing point, evolution of temperature in the specimens at different elevations, water content distributions and cryostructures after freezing, frost heave during freezing, and state paths. In this regard, a physico-empirical approach is developed to obtain the relationship between freezing point and initial water contents. Experimental data show that the freezing point of expansive clay varies greatly with initial water contents. The obvious highly exothermic phase change occurs in expansive clay during the early stage of freezing with penetration decrease lagging behind. The heave amount of expansive clay is made up of the displacement caused by increasing water content in the unfrozen zone due to freezing-induced water flux and the frost heave. The state paths show significant variation of saturation and dry density of expansive clay after freezing and have a practical advantage of indicating the extent of possible expansion while thawing. On this basis, the state and variation of pore water are highlighted as the critical primary factors in determining the frost heave characteristics of unsaturated expansive clay in open system. Overall, this study further enhances the understanding of frost heave characteristics of the unsaturated moderately expansive clay. The lowest temperature in many regions is less than 0 °C, and can even reach −40 °C. The expansive clays in these areas can produce frost heave, causing costly damages to infrastructures as a result of a sophisticated process with both frost heaving and crystalline swelling. Numerous studies have attempted to explain the frost heave characteristics of clayey soils (Taber, 1930; Beskow, 1935; Konrad and Morgenstern, 1980; Konrad and Seto, 1994; Han and Goodings, 2006; Azmatch et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2014; Hendry et al., 2016; She et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2018). However, few of them have paid attention to the frost heave characteristics of unsaturated expansive clay, especially considering the influence of swelling properties. When the soil temperature drops to the freezing point below 0 °C, the crystallization of pore water can occur with the release of latent heat, and then the frost heave is likely to happen. Previous experimental results indicate that the freezing point of clayey soil with the nearly saturated water content is slightly below 0 °C. Only when the clayey soil is dry enough can the freezing point become very low. Progressive researches of the relationship between freezing point and pore water content have been conducted frequently (Anderson and Tice, 1972; Jame and Norum, 1972; Kozlowski, 2004; Watanabe and Flury, 2008; Kurylyk and Watanabe, 2013; Liu and Yu, 2014). Meanwhile, a few experimental studies have shown that the bentonite with the relatively high water content, containing a large amount of montmorillonites and being purified from solutes, can also possess a very low freezing point (Kozlowski, 2004; Kozlowski, 2009; Kozlowski, 2016). It is well accepted in the profession that the expansive clay is dominated by a large amount of clay minerals, mainly montmorillonites. The clay minerals can adsorb abundant cations, such as Na+, K+, H+, Ca2+ and Mg2+, which may influence the freezing point of expansive clay. Until now, very few freezing temperature tests of expansive clay and related theoretical analyses have been undertaken. Significant frost heave is usually due to the water migration and accumulation (Taber, 1929, Taber, 1930). A few previous studies have provided evidence for the dramatic freezing-induced water migration in unsaturated soils (Dirksen and Miller, 1966; Jame, 1977; Konrad, 2008). In a closed system, the increase of water content of the frozen soil with time took place over an extended zone beyond the 0 °C isotherm (Dirksen and Miller, 1966). In an open system, the water content near the freezing front and the unfrozen zone both increased, especially in the former (Konrad, 2008). Recent experimental evidences find that vapor flow could be a dominant mechanism of water migration in freezing unsaturated soils (Eigenbrod and Kennepohl, 1996; Zhang et al., 2016; He et al., 2018). Considering the canopy effect, it is found that vapor transfer can lead to significant water and ice accumulation near the freezing end where the total water content is close to full saturation (Zhang et al., 2016). While the widespread use of agricultural machinery has improved field operation efficiency, it has also made soil compaction a particularly prominent issue under intensive farming (Batey, 2009, Shah et al., 2017, Tracy et al., 2011). Soil structure has a significant influence on soil physical properties and is a key indicator of soil health (Ma et al., 2024, Peng et al., 2024, Yuan and Fan, 2024). The degradation of soil structure caused by compaction will have lasting negative impacts on soil ecological functions (such as the retention and flow of water, gases, heat, and nutrients) for decades (Pulido-Moncada et al., 2019, Ten Damme et al., 2021, Zhang and Peng, 2021). These negative effects hinder root growth, suppress plant development, and ultimately lead to reduced crop yields (Beutler et al., 2021, Liu et al., 2022, Pandey et al., 2021, Wang et al., 2022, Yue et al., 2021). Therefore, assessing changes in soil structure under intensive farming helps to better understand the impact of soil compaction on soil health. As agricultural machinery continues to increase in size and weight, coupled with the growing frequency of agricultural activities, studying soil structure under different compaction levels is crucial for sustainable development and soil environmental protection. Due to the opacity of soil, X-ray computed tomography (CT) technology is considered an effective method for studying soil structure, thanks to its advantages of non-destructive measurement, multi-parameter acquisition, and 3D reconstruction (Budhathoki et al., 2022, Carducci et al., 2017, Dhaliwal and Kumar, 2022, Pagenkemper et al., 2015). Some studies have extensively explored pore deformation in soil caused by compaction using CT (Feng et al., 2020, Goldberg-Yehuda et al., 2024, Mossadeghi-Björklund et al., 2016). Quantitative CT data offer valuable insights into the microstructural changes in soil resulting from compaction processes. Soil compaction disturbs the soil pore system and alters the pore size distribution, pore geometry and morphology, and pore connectivity (Feng et al., 2019, Goldberg-Yehuda et al., 2022). Most current studies primarily simulate compaction by adjusting bulk density, using laboratory-simulated manual presses, or employing a single machine for continuous wheeling (Feng et al., 2020, Goldberg-Yehuda et al., 2024, Goldberg-Yehuda et al., 2022). However, due to subtle differences in particle size and shape, stresses in soil do not propagate homogeneously but instead follow preferential paths in all directions (Majmudar and Behringer, 2005). Under natural conditions, freeze-thaw cycles are one of the primary natural drivers in alleviating compacted soil structure (Jabro et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020). Freeze-thaw cycles can alter soil structure by disrupting soil aggregates and changing the arrangement and bonding of soil particles through water-induced shrink-swell of pore spaces (Huang et al., 2021, Zhang et al., 2016). In this process, the pore system of soil structure shows a significant response to freeze-thaw cycles. Previous research has comprehensively evaluated changes in soil pore structure under different freeze-thaw cycles using CT scanning technology (Liu et al., 2023a, Liu et al., 2023b, Liu et al., 2021b, Liu et al., 2021a, Ma et al., 2021). The relationship between pore structure and aggregate stability has been explored, offering valuable insights into the effects of freeze-thaw cycles on soil. However, these studies were conducted under controlled laboratory conditions and overlooked the influence of pre-freeze-thaw soil compaction. Under the influence of external forces, changes in soil pore characteristics are closely related to the stability of aggregates (Peng et al., 2023, Wu and Hu, 2024, Zhang et al., 2024b). Freeze-thaw cycles damage soil through water migration and ice formation. It also says that compaction compresses macropores into smaller micropores, reducing pore connectivity and creating a dense structure dominated by micropores [N5-F1]. After thaw, this pre-existing microstructure influences how the soil reconsolidates. If the soil was already compacted, thaw settlement may be less pronounced in absolute terms because there is less available pore space to collapse, but the remaining structure may still be more prone to delayed consolidation or residual compression [N5-F1][N6-R1]. The compaction literature also implies that soil structure and pore connectivity are key to aggregate stability and mechanical response [N5-F1], so compaction can modify whether the soil rebounds strongly, settles gradually, or remains damaged after thaw.

Frost damage severity can be reduced or exacerbated during thaw depending on the compaction level and prior freeze-thaw history. The evidence suggests that thaw settlement is associated with high pore pressures and consolidation during thawing [N6-R3]. This means that if a soil was already compacted before freezing, the thaw process may release stored pore pressures more rapidly, potentially reducing residual damage in some cases. However, if the compaction level was so high that the soil had already lost much of its pore space, thawing may not have much room to settle and could leave the soil in a more compacted, less recoverable state. The freeze-thaw literature also indicates that repeated cycles degrade soil structure, increase heterogeneity, and reduce bearing capacity during thaw [N2-F3][N2-R1]. Therefore, the compaction history matters: soils that were compacted before freezing may show less dramatic thaw settlement, but their damage severity may not be fully recovered because the freeze-thaw process already altered the microstructure and mechanical properties [N5-F1][N2-F3].

## Integrated conclusion

So the overall picture is that soil compaction affects soil strength and frost damage after freeze-thaw cycles in a complex, bidirectional way. Compaction increases dry density and reduces porosity, which improves shear strength and bearing capacity but also alters water retention and hydraulic conductivity [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N5-F1]. At the same time, compaction reduces frost heave magnitude and thaw settlement by limiting pore space and connectivity [N1-R2][N5-F1]. But compaction does not eliminate frost damage entirely: it can change crack propagation, damage severity, and the way the soil responds to freeze-thaw stress [N5-F1][N4-F2]. After thaw, soils with different compaction levels recover differently, with thaw settlement and post-frost strength recovery depending on residual pore structure and reconsolidation behavior [N6-R1][N6-R3]. Frost damage severity can be reduced or exacerbated during thaw, depending on how compaction interacts with thaw-induced consolidation and prior freeze-thaw degradation [N5-F1][N2-F3][N6-R3].

In practical terms, this means that soil compaction is not a neutral factor. It can help reduce frost damage by making the soil denser and less porous, but it can also make the soil more difficult to recover after thaw because the microstructure and pore connectivity have already changed [N5-F1][N6-R1]. The degree of compaction therefore matters because it modifies frost heave magnitude, thaw settlement, crack propagation, and the long-term strength and damage behavior of the soil [N1-R2][N5-F1][N4-F2][N2-F3].
